youtube.title: US Invaded Canada Twice: The 8,891 km Line That Survived Both
youtube.description:
The United States invaded Canada in 1775 and again in 1812. Both times the armies withdrew, and the border came back almost where it was. So why did two invasions fail to move the longest border between any two countries, and why is that line being questioned again today?

We follow the 8,891 km line on the map: Arnold's march through Maine, the fall of Detroit, the burning of York and Washington, the Treaty of Ghent, the lake treaty that took the warships away, and the 49th parallel. Then the rivalry now, in tariffs, fentanyl figures and Arctic water, with each side's case in its own terms, and three ways the pressure on the line could play out.

{CHAPTERS}

youtube.comment: If you live near the US–Canada border, which crossing do you use most, and how long is the wait? 👇

sources.claim: The Canada–US border is 8,891 km long, the longest between two countries
sources.source: International Boundary Commission, 'The Boundary' (IBC website, accessed 2026)

sources.claim: 6,416 km across the continent and 2,475 km between Alaska and Canada
sources.source: International Boundary Commission, boundary length by section

sources.claim: A six-metre (20 ft) vista is kept cleared along the boundary
sources.source: International Boundary Commission, 'Vista clearing'; Treaty of 1925 between the US and Great Britain

sources.claim: About 60 percent of US crude oil imports come from Canada
sources.source: US Energy Information Administration, 'Where our oil comes from' (2023 data)

sources.claim: The 49th parallel section runs more than 2,000 km from Lake of the Woods to the Strait of Georgia
sources.source: International Boundary Commission, boundary sections; Convention of 1818 and Oregon Treaty 1846

sources.claim: Detroit is the busiest port on the US–Canada border by trade value
sources.source: US Bureau of Transportation Statistics, TransBorder Freight Data, 2024

sources.claim: Much of Detroit's border trade is carried by truck over the Ambassador Bridge
sources.source: US Bureau of Transportation Statistics, TransBorder Freight Data 2024, Detroit port by mode (truck the largest share); Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority, Gordie Howe International Bridge project background on Ambassador Bridge truck traffic

sources.claim: Montreal is Canada's second-largest city
sources.source: Statistics Canada, 2021 Census of Population (City of Montréal 1,762,949, second to Toronto)

sources.claim: Montreal is about 50 km in a straight line from the US border
sources.source: Measured on Natural Resources Canada Atlas of Canada base map

sources.claim: Canada's population about 41.7 million
sources.source: Statistics Canada, population estimate 1 July 2025

sources.claim: US population about 340 million
sources.source: US Census Bureau, Vintage 2024 population estimate (1 July 2024)

sources.claim: Roughly 380 million people in Canada and the US together
sources.source: Sum of Statistics Canada (41.7 million, 1 July 2025) and US Census Bureau (about 340 million, 1 July 2024) estimates

sources.claim: Machias Seal Island is claimed by both countries; Canada has kept a staffed lighthouse there since the 1830s (1832)
sources.source: Canadian Coast Guard lighthouse records; US Department of State, Limits in the Seas / CRS reports on US–Canada boundary disputes

sources.claim: A wedge of the Beaufort Sea is disputed: Canada extends the 141st meridian, the US uses an equidistance line
sources.source: Government of Canada, Global Affairs Canada Arctic policy; US Department of State statements on the Beaufort Sea boundary

sources.claim: Canada calls the Northwest Passage internal waters; the US calls it a strait used for international navigation
sources.source: Government of Canada, Arctic Foreign Policy (2024); US Department of State, 2019 statements on the Northwest Passage

sources.claim: Quebec passed from France to Britain in 1763
sources.source: Treaty of Paris, 10 February 1763

sources.claim: Twelve years between the cession of 1763 and the invasion of 1775
sources.source: Derived: Treaty of Paris, 10 February 1763; US Army Center of Military History, 'The Invasion of Canada, 1775–1776' (invasion began September 1775)

sources.claim: The Quebec Act of 1774 guaranteed free exercise of the Catholic religion and restored French civil law
sources.source: Quebec Act, 14 Geo. III c. 83 (1774), sections V and VIII

sources.claim: The Continental Congress wrote to the inhabitants of Quebec inviting them to join
sources.source: Journals of the Continental Congress, letters of 26 October 1774 and 29 May 1775

sources.claim: Montgomery besieged Fort Saint-Jean from 17 September to 2 November 1775, close to seven weeks; Montreal fell on 13 November 1775
sources.source: US Army Center of Military History, 'The Invasion of Canada, 1775–1776'; Parks Canada, Fort Saint-Jean (duration derived from the siege dates, about 46 days)

sources.claim: Arnold's march up the Kennebec ran about 560 km (350 miles) and took about six weeks
sources.source: Thomas A. Desjardin, 'Through a Howling Wilderness' (2006); National Park Service, Arnold Trail to Quebec

sources.claim: About 1,100 men set out with Arnold and about 600 reached the St. Lawrence; counts differ between march diarists
sources.source: Desjardin (2006); Justin H. Smith, 'Arnold's March from Cambridge to Quebec' (1903)

sources.claim: Attack on Quebec City on 31 December 1775 in a snowstorm; Montgomery killed, Arnold wounded, more than 400 Americans captured
sources.source: US Army Center of Military History, 'The Invasion of Canada, 1775–1776'; Canadian Encyclopedia, 'Battle of Quebec (1775)'

sources.claim: British reinforcements reached Quebec in May 1776; Americans withdrew to Lake Champlain by July 1776
sources.source: US Army Center of Military History; Canadian Encyclopedia, 'American Invasion of Canada 1775–1776'

sources.claim: Articles of Confederation, Article XI: Canada could join without the consent of nine states
sources.source: Articles of Confederation, agreed 15 November 1777, ratified 1 March 1781, Article XI

sources.claim: Treaty of Paris 1783 drew the line through the Great Lakes to Lake of the Woods
sources.source: Treaty of Paris, 3 September 1783, Article II

sources.claim: British troops held posts on the US side, including Detroit, until 1796
sources.source: Jay Treaty, 19 November 1794, Article II; US Office of the Historian

sources.claim: The US declared war on Britain on 18 June 1812
sources.source: Act of Congress declaring war, signed 18 June 1812; US Office of the Historian

sources.claim: Madison's war message accused Britain of impressing sailors from American ships and blockading American trade
sources.source: James Madison, Special Message to Congress, 1 June 1812

sources.claim: Britain said it was recovering deserters from the Royal Navy
sources.source: Donald R. Hickey, 'The War of 1812: A Forgotten Conflict' (2012 ed.)

sources.claim: Native nations allied around Tecumseh said they were defending their lands
sources.source: Alan Taylor, 'The Civil War of 1812' (2010); Canadian Encyclopedia, 'Tecumseh'

sources.claim: US population 7.2 million in 1810
sources.source: US Census Bureau, 1810 Census (7,239,881)

sources.claim: British North America had roughly half a million people in 1812; estimates vary
sources.source: Hickey (2012); Canadian Encyclopedia, 'War of 1812'

sources.claim: Hull crossed into Upper Canada on 12 July 1812, pulled back to Detroit in early August, and surrendered Detroit to Brock and Tecumseh on 16 August 1812
sources.source: Canadian Encyclopedia, 'Capture of Detroit'; Hickey (2012)

sources.claim: Jefferson: Canada 'a mere matter of marching'
sources.source: Thomas Jefferson to William Duane, 4 August 1812, Founders Online (National Archives)

sources.claim: After the surrender, Detroit and most of Michigan Territory passed under British control
sources.source: Hickey (2012); Canadian Encyclopedia, 'Capture of Detroit'

sources.claim: American crossing at Queenston Heights failed on 13 October 1812; Brock was killed
sources.source: Parks Canada, Queenston Heights National Historic Site

sources.claim: American forces captured York on 27 April 1813 and burned its parliament buildings
sources.source: Canadian Encyclopedia, 'Battle of York'; City of Toronto Museums, Fort York

sources.claim: Perry won the Battle of Lake Erie on 10 September 1813
sources.source: National Park Service, Perry's Victory and International Peace Memorial

sources.claim: Americans retook Detroit in September 1813; Tecumseh was killed at the Thames on 5 October 1813
sources.source: Canadian Encyclopedia, 'Battle of the Thames'; Hickey (2012)

sources.claim: American advances on Montreal turned back at Châteauguay (26 October 1813) and Crysler's Farm (11 November 1813)
sources.source: Parks Canada, Battle of the Châteauguay and Battle of Crysler's Farm National Historic Sites

sources.claim: Napoleon abdicated in April 1814
sources.source: Treaty of Fontainebleau, 11 April 1814 (abdication 6 April 1814)

sources.claim: Lundy's Lane, 25 July 1814, both sides claimed success; the front stayed on the Niagara River
sources.source: Canadian Encyclopedia, 'Battle of Lundy's Lane'; Hickey (2012)

sources.claim: British troops burned the Capitol and the President's House on 24 August 1814, then withdrew to their ships on the coast
sources.source: White House Historical Association; Hickey (2012)

sources.claim: British advance south by Lake Champlain withdrew after the naval defeat at Plattsburgh, 11 September 1814
sources.source: US Naval History and Heritage Command, 'Battle of Lake Champlain'

sources.claim: Wellington: 'you have no right, from the state of the war, to demand any concession of territory from America'
sources.source: Duke of Wellington to Lord Liverpool, 9 November 1814, Supplementary Despatches vol. 9

sources.claim: Treaty of Ghent signed 24 December 1814, restoring captured territory
sources.source: Treaty of Ghent, 24 December 1814, Article I

sources.claim: Article IX promised Native nations their 1811 possessions; historians say it went largely unkept
sources.source: Treaty of Ghent, Article IX; Alan Taylor (2010); Colin Calloway, 'Crown and Calumet' (1987)

sources.claim: Rush–Bagot agreement, 1817: one armed vessel on Lake Ontario, two on the upper lakes, one on Lake Champlain
sources.source: Rush–Bagot Agreement, exchange of notes 28–29 April 1817; US Office of the Historian

sources.claim: 1818: 49th parallel from Lake of the Woods to the Rocky Mountains
sources.source: Convention of 1818, 20 October 1818, Article II

sources.claim: Rideau Canal, 202 km, opened 1832 as a military supply route
sources.source: Parks Canada, Rideau Canal National Historic Site; UNESCO World Heritage listing (2007)

sources.claim: Queen Victoria chose Ottawa as capital in 1857; distance from the border among the reasons cited
sources.source: Library and Archives Canada; Canadian Encyclopedia, 'Ottawa' (Sir Edmund Head memorandum, 1857)

sources.claim: About 31,000 km² (12,000 sq mi) disputed in Maine; standoff in the Aroostook valley in 1839 without a battle
sources.source: US Office of the Historian, 'The Webster-Ashburton Treaty, 1842'

sources.claim: Webster–Ashburton Treaty 1842 split the land, about 18,000 km² to the US and 13,000 km² to Britain
sources.source: US Office of the Historian, 'The Webster-Ashburton Treaty, 1842' (7,015 and 5,012 sq mi)

sources.claim: The Oregon Country was shared from 1818; slogan '54-40 or fight'
sources.source: US Office of the Historian, 'The Oregon Territory, 1846'

sources.claim: 1846 Oregon Treaty: 49th parallel, all of Vancouver Island to Britain
sources.source: Oregon Treaty, 15 June 1846, Article I

sources.claim: Fenian raids of 1866 by Irish-American Civil War veterans, without US government backing; raiders withdrew within days and the border did not change
sources.source: Canadian Encyclopedia, 'Fenian Raids'; Library and Archives Canada

sources.claim: US bought Alaska for 7.2 million dollars in 1867; Canada confederated on 1 July 1867
sources.source: Treaty with Russia, 30 March 1867 (National Archives); Constitution Act, 1867

sources.claim: 1903 Alaska boundary tribunal largely backed the US claim
sources.source: US Office of the Historian, 'The Alaska Boundary Dispute'

sources.claim: Joint boundary commission from 1908, made permanent by the 1925 treaty
sources.source: Treaty of 11 April 1908; Treaty of 24 February 1925; International Boundary Commission

sources.claim: Trump, 7 January 2025: 'get rid of that artificially drawn line'; asked about military force on Canada, he ruled it out: 'No, economic force'
sources.source: Press conference at Mar-a-Lago, 7 January 2025 (questions covered Greenland, Panama and Canada), reported by Associated Press and Reuters

sources.claim: Trump repeatedly called Canada a potential 51st state in 2025; Canadian party leaders rejected it
sources.source: CBC News and Reuters reporting, January–May 2025

sources.claim: 4 March 2025: US 25 percent tariffs on many Canadian goods, citing fentanyl and border security
sources.source: White House executive order, 1 February 2025, effective 4 March 2025

sources.claim: Canada's same-day counter-tariffs on C$30 billion of US goods, including orange juice and appliances
sources.source: Department of Finance Canada, 4 March 2025

sources.claim: 2024 US goods imports from Canada 412.7 billion dollars; exports 349.4 billion dollars
sources.source: US Census Bureau, Trade in Goods with Canada, 2024

sources.claim: Many Midwest refineries are configured to run Canadian heavy crude
sources.source: US Energy Information Administration, PADD 2 refinery crude slate analyses (2023–2024)

sources.claim: US Customs seized about 43 lb of fentanyl at the northern border and about 21,100 lb at the southwest border in fiscal 2024
sources.source: US Customs and Border Protection, Drug Seizure Statistics, FY2024

sources.claim: Canada named a fentanyl czar and added border spending
sources.source: Prime Minister of Canada, 11 February 2025 (fentanyl czar); Public Safety Canada, C$1.3 billion border plan, 17 December 2024

sources.claim: In June 2025 Canada said it would meet NATO's 2 percent target that year
sources.source: Prime Minister Mark Carney announcement, 9 June 2025

sources.claim: Carney, 6 May 2025: 'there are some places that are never for sale'; Trump: 'Never say never'
sources.source: Oval Office meeting, 6 May 2025, White House transcript; CNN and CBC reporting

sources.claim: Car parts can cross the border several times before a vehicle is finished
sources.source: Center for Automotive Research; Canadian Vehicle Manufacturers' Association (2025)

sources.claim: USMCA signed in 2018, in force 1 July 2020, first joint review in July 2026
sources.source: USMCA, signed 30 November 2018, Article 34.7 (joint review on the sixth anniversary of entry into force, 1 July 2026); USTR

sources.claim: In 1969 the tanker SS Manhattan transited the Northwest Passage with Canadian permission, escorted by the Canadian icebreaker CCGS John A. Macdonald
sources.source: Adam Lajeunesse, 'Lock, Stock, and Icebergs: A History of Canada's Arctic Maritime Sovereignty' (UBC Press, 2016); Elizabeth B. Elliot-Meisel, 'Still Unresolved after Fifty Years: The Northwest Passage in Canadian-American Relations, 1946–1998', American Review of Canadian Studies 29:3 (1999)

sources.claim: In 1985 the USCGC Polar Sea transited without requesting Canadian consent, setting off the sovereignty row that led to the 1988 agreement
sources.source: Secretary of State for External Affairs Joe Clark, statement in the House of Commons, 10 September 1985 (Hansard); Lajeunesse (2016); Elliot-Meisel (1999)

sources.claim: 1988 Arctic Cooperation Agreement: US icebreakers seek consent, without prejudice to either legal position
sources.source: Agreement on Arctic Cooperation, 11 January 1988

sources.claim: September Arctic sea ice has shrunk by roughly 13 percent a decade since 1979
sources.source: National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC), Arctic Sea Ice News, September 2024

sources.claim: By many analysts' account, pressure on the US–Canada relationship rose in 2025
sources.source: Reuters, CBC News and policy-institute commentary on US–Canada relations, 2025

sources.claim: Canada's government says it will widen its export markets beyond the US
sources.source: Prime Minister Mark Carney, statements on trade diversification, 2025; Government of Canada, Budget 2025 (4 November 2025)

sources.claim: Trans Mountain expansion in service May 2024, capacity 890,000 barrels a day
sources.source: Trans Mountain Corporation, 1 May 2024; Canada Energy Regulator

sources.claim: Before the Trans Mountain expansion, almost all Canadian crude exports went to the United States
sources.source: Canada Energy Regulator, crude oil export statistics and Market Snapshots on post-expansion exports (2024)

sources.claim: Canada–EU trade deal (CETA) in force provisionally since 2017; the US buys about three quarters of Canadian exports
sources.source: Global Affairs Canada (CETA, 21 September 2017); Statistics Canada, merchandise trade 2024

sources.claim: NORAD joint command since 1958, headquartered in Colorado with a Canadian region headquarters in Winnipeg
sources.source: NORAD official history (12 May 1958); Department of National Defence

sources.claim: Treaties of 1818, 1846 and 1908 remain in force
sources.source: US Department of State, Treaties in Force (2024); Global Affairs Canada Treaty Law database

sources.claim: Historians most often credit treaties and demilitarisation for holding the line
sources.source: US Office of the Historian, 'Rush-Bagot Pact, 1817 and 1818'; Hickey (2012); Canadian Encyclopedia, 'Rush–Bagot Agreement'

sources.claim: A US president has said he wants to buy Greenland
sources.source: Reuters and AP reporting, August 2019 and January 2025
